def: To give up something valuable in order to obtain something more important.
ex: She had to sacrifice her weekends to complete the software certification on schedule.
nat: Parents often sacrifice their personal ambitions for the wellbeing of their children.

mis.bad: He sacrificed of his free time for work.
mis.good: He sacrificed his free time for work.
mis.why: Do not put "of" after "sacrifice"; it is a transitive verb.

def: Most noticeable or important.
ex: The summary outlines the most salient points from this morning strategy session.
nat: He highlighted the salient features of the proposed database migration.

mis.bad: These are the salients points of the report.
mis.good: These are the salient points of the report.
mis.why: English adjectives never take a plural "-s".

def: To rescue or save something from potential loss or total destruction.
ex: The engineers managed to salvage the corrupted database after working all night.
nat: We can still salvage this customer relationship if we act very quickly.

mis.bad: We could not salvage nothing from the crash.
mis.good: We could not salvage anything from the crash.
mis.why: Avoid double negatives: use "anything" rather than "nothing" after "not".

def: The ability to think and behave in a normal and rational manner.
ex: Taking short daily walks in the afternoon helps me maintain my sanity.
nat: For the sake of your sanity, turn off work notifications on weekends.

mis.bad: I need a sanity test before deploying.
mis.good: I need to run a sanity check before deploying.
mis.why: In software engineering, the common phrase is "sanity check", not "sanity test".

def: To fill something completely so that no more can be added.
ex: Heavy summer rainfall can quickly saturate the soil along the mountain highway.
nat: Too many discount brands have started to saturate the regional retail market.

mis.bad: The market is saturated of low quality gadgets.
mis.good: The market is saturated with low quality gadgets.
mis.why: Use the preposition "with" after "saturated", not "of".

def: To walk in a slow, relaxed, and casual manner.
ex: Tourists often saunter through the historic cobblestone streets in the late afternoon.
nat: He casually sauntered into the lecture hall ten minutes late.

mis.bad: We sauntered fast to catch the train.
mis.good: We hurried to catch the train.
mis.why: "Saunter" means walking slowly and leisurely, never quickly.

def: Having practical knowledge, experience, and good common sense.
ex: A savvy investor always diversifies risk across different international asset classes.
nat: She is extremely tech savvy and builds automated workflows effortlessly.

mis.bad: He is very savvy about computer.
mis.good: He is very tech-savvy / savvy with computers.
mis.why: Combine "savvy" directly as a compound word (tech-savvy) or use "with".

def: A temporary structure used to support workers or code during development.
ex: Construction workers carefully erected a sturdy scaffold around the exterior walls.
nat: The framework command generated a scaffold for our user authentication module.

mis.bad: They putted an scaffold on the front.
mis.good: They put a scaffold on the front.
mis.why: Past tense of "put" is "put", not "putted".

def: Barely sufficient or adequate in amount or degree.
ex: The project team paid scant attention to documentation during the initial release.
nat: There is scant evidence that this marketing experiment drove any subscriptions.

mis.bad: We have a scant of money.
mis.good: We have scant money.
mis.why: Do not use "of" after "scant"; use it directly before the noun.

def: To throw or distribute things in various random directions.
ex: A sudden gust of wind scattered the paperwork across the entire parking lot.
nat: The crowd quickly scattered when heavy thunder began to rumble overhead.

mis.bad: She scattered the toys on everywhere.
mis.good: She scattered the toys everywhere.
mis.why: Do not use "on" before "everywhere".

def: A diagram or plan that explains the components of a complex system.
ex: The hardware engineer examined the schematic carefully before ordering the circuit boards.
nat: This schematic illustrates how traffic flows between our microservices and database.

mis.bad: I drew a schematic to explain the system.
mis.good: I drew a schematic to explain the system.
mis.why: Remember that "schematic" has the "k" sound: /skiːˈmætɪk/.

def: Involving or relating to serious academic study and intellectual rigor.
ex: She published several scholarly articles on natural language processing in reputable journals.
nat: The library has an impressive collection of scholarly books on linguistics.

mis.bad: He writes very scholarly.
mis.good: He writes in a scholarly way / writes scholarly papers.
mis.why: "Scholarly" is an adjective; use "in a scholarly manner" as an adverb.

def: To burn the surface of something with intense fire or heat.
ex: The hot summer sun began to scorch the grass across the front yard.
nat: High temperatures will scorch delicate fabrics if you do not lower the iron.

mis.bad: The fire scorched down the entire house.
mis.good: The fire burned down the entire house.
mis.why: "Scorch" means superficial burning; for total destruction use "burn down".

def: The feeling or belief that someone or something is despicable or worthless.
ex: His careless attitude toward code quality was met with scorn from senior developers.
nat: She poured scorn on the proposal during the executive committee meeting.

mis.bad: He feels scorn by her.
mis.good: He feels scorn for her / feels scorned by her.
mis.why: Use "scorn for [someone]" as a noun, or "scorned by" as a passive verb.

def: To search thoroughly or scrub a surface vigorously to clean it.
ex: Investigators had to scour through thousands of server logs to locate the anomaly.
nat: You should scour the frying pan with a sponge to remove the grease.

mis.bad: We scoured at the code to find bugs.
mis.good: We scoured the code to find bugs.
mis.why: "Scour" takes a direct object without the preposition "at".

def: To move hurriedly or clumsily, or scramble data into random order.
ex: The operations team had to scramble quickly when the payment gateway went down.
nat: He likes to scramble eggs with a pinch of fresh parsley every morning.

mis.bad: They scrambled to the meeting room running.
mis.good: They scrambled into the meeting room.
mis.why: Avoid redundant adverbs like "running" with "scrambled".

def: To write or draw something carelessly or in a hurry.
ex: I had to scribble his contact details on a napkin before leaving.
nat: She scribbled some notes in the margin while listening to the webinar.

mis.bad: He scribbled at the paper quickly.
mis.good: He scribbled on the paper quickly.
mis.why: Use "on" or "down", not "at", with "scribble".

def: To keep someone or oneself away from other people or distractions.
ex: The author decided to seclude himself in a rustic cabin to finish writing.
nat: Students often seclude themselves in quiet study pods before major final exams.

mis.bad: He secluded of the community.
mis.good: He secluded himself from the community.
mis.why: Use the reflexive pronoun with "seclude oneself from".

def: Sheltered or private; not easily seen or visited by many people.
ex: They rented a secluded cottage near the lake for their anniversary weekend.
nat: The hotel beach is secluded and surrounded by tall pine trees.

mis.bad: The place is secluded from people visits.
mis.good: The place is secluded from crowds / quiet and secluded.
mis.why: Use "secluded" alone to describe quiet, private places.

def: Not connected with religious or spiritual matters; worldly.
ex: Most Western democracies uphold a secular system of government and public education.
nat: The university maintains a strictly secular curriculum for all undergraduate degrees.

mis.bad: Brazil has an secular state.
mis.good: Brazil has a secular state.
mis.why: Use the indefinite article "a" before consonant sounds: "a secular state".

def: Each of the parts into which something is divided or can be separated.
ex: The corporate banking segment delivered the strongest revenue growth during the third quarter.
nat: Marketing teams analyze each user segment to tailor promotional campaigns effectively.

mis.bad: We divided the market in segments.
mis.good: We divided the market into segments.
mis.why: Use "divide into segments", not "divide in segments".

def: To isolate or divide groups, data, or materials from each other.
ex: Modern cloud architects segregate sensitive customer credentials from public application networks.
nat: The laboratory strictly segregates hazardous biological chemicals from regular household garbage.

mis.bad: The system segregates data with user roles.
mis.good: The system segregates data by user roles.
mis.why: Use "segregate by [criteria]" or "segregate A from B".

def: To take hold of suddenly and forcibly, or capture an opportunity eagerly.
ex: Young entrepreneurs should seize this opportunity to launch products in overseas markets.
nat: Customs officers at the border seized several counterfeit shipments this morning.

mis.bad: You must to seize the chance.
mis.good: You must seize the chance.
mis.why: Modal verbs like "must" take the bare infinitive without "to".

def: Tending to choose carefully, or affecting only certain things or people.
ex: Top technology universities are extremely selective about which applicants receive graduate funding.
nat: He is very selective when picking freelance consulting contracts each quarter.

mis.bad: The company is very selective for candidates.
mis.good: The company is very selective about candidates.
mis.why: Use "selective about" rather than "selective for".

def: A punctuation mark (;) indicating a pause longer than a comma.
ex: In JavaScript, many developers choose to omit the semicolon at line ends.
nat: A semicolon connects two independent clauses that are closely related in meaning.

mis.bad: I forgot the semicolon in the line end.
mis.good: I forgot the semicolon at the end of the line.
mis.why: Use "at the end of the line", not "in the line end".

def: Causing great public interest and excitement, or extraordinarily good.
ex: The symphony orchestra gave a sensational performance of Beethoven Ninth Symphony last night.
nat: Tabloid newspapers often print sensational headlines simply to drive clicks.

mis.bad: The concert was so much sensational.
mis.good: The concert was sensational / truly sensational.
mis.why: Do not use "so much" to modify adjectives; use "so" or "truly".

def: A view of or attitude toward a situation; or general opinion.
ex: Consumer sentiment improved significantly after the central bank lowered domestic interest rates.
nat: The analysis tool monitors public sentiment across popular social networks in real-time.

mis.bad: The sentiment of the people are positive.
mis.good: The sentiment of the people is positive.
mis.why: "Sentiment" is a singular noun and requires a singular verb ("is").

def: Prompted by feelings of tenderness, sadness, or nostalgic affection.
ex: This antique gold watch has enormous sentimental value because my grandfather wore it.
nat: She felt sentimental when looking through old photographs from her university days.

mis.bad: That watch has a big sentimental valor.
mis.good: That watch has great sentimental value.
mis.why: Use the English word "value", not Portuguese "valor".

def: A particular order in which related events, movements, or things follow each other.
ex: Make sure the startup scripts execute in the exact sequence specified in documentation.
nat: Scientists decoded the complete genetic sequence of the newly discovered deep-sea coral.

mis.bad: Execute the tasks in the right sequential.
mis.good: Execute the tasks in the right sequence.
mis.why: Use the noun "sequence" after an adjective like "right", not "sequential".

def: Forming or following in a logical or ordered sequence.
ex: The batch pipeline processes customer transactions through three sequential data verification stages.
nat: Learning grammar requires a sequential approach rather than jumping randomly between topics.

mis.bad: The system executes sequential the tasks.
mis.good: The system executes the tasks sequentially.
mis.why: Use the adverb "sequentially" to modify the verb "executes".

def: Calm, peaceful, and untroubled; tranquil.
ex: The mountain resort offered a serene atmosphere away from busy city life.
nat: She remained remarkably serene throughout the intense contract negotiation meeting.

mis.bad: I felt very serene with the nature.
mis.good: I felt very serene in nature.
mis.why: Say "in nature", not "with the nature".

def: The state of being calm, peaceful, and untroubled.
ex: Practicing mindfulness meditation every morning brings a profound sense of inner serenity.
nat: The undisturbed serenity of the forest was broken only by chirping birds.

mis.bad: I love the serenity from this beach.
mis.good: I love the serenity of this beach.
mis.why: Use "serenity of [a place]", not "from".

def: Arranged in or occurring as a series, or publishing in installments.
ex: Serial entrepreneurship requires resilience and the ability to pivot when markets shift.
nat: Every manufactured computer motherboard is stamped with a unique serial number.

mis.bad: The device has a number serial printed on back.
mis.good: The device has a serial number printed on the back.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "serial number", not "number serial".

def: To divide by cutting, or put an end to a connection or relationship.
ex: The consulting firm decided to sever business ties after repeated invoice nonpayment.
nat: A construction backhoe accidentally severed the underground fiber optic internet cable.

mis.bad: They severed with the supplier.
mis.good: They severed ties with the supplier.
mis.why: "Sever" is transitive; specify what is cut (e.g., "sever ties").

def: Of little depth; lacking intellectual or emotional substance.
ex: Children can safely splash in the shallow end of the outdoor swimming pool.
nat: His critique of the novel felt shallow and ignored its deeper themes.

mis.bad: The water is very shallow to dive.
mis.good: The water is too shallow to dive in.
mis.why: Use "too shallow to [verb]", not "very shallow to".

def: To break or cause something to break suddenly and violently into pieces.
ex: The sudden economic recession threatened to shatter consumer confidence across the retail sector.
nat: Falling rocks shattered the windshield of the delivery truck yesterday.

mis.bad: The loud sound shattered with my concentration.
mis.good: The loud sound shattered my concentration.
mis.why: "Shatter" is transitive and does not take "with".

def: To cut the wool off a sheep, or break off due to structural stress.
ex: High lateral wind forces can easily shear bolts on exposed solar panel mounts.
nat: Farmers gather every spring to shear their sheep before the summer heat arrives.

mis.bad: The bolt sheared off by the strong pressure.
mis.good: The bolt sheared off due to high pressure.
mis.why: Use "due to" or "under" high pressure.

def: To get rid of something no longer needed, or cast off naturally.
ex: The struggling technology company had to shed hundreds of non-core operational jobs.
nat: Deciduous trees shed their dry leaves before the freezing winter weather begins.

mis.bad: The article sheds a light about this problem.
mis.good: The article sheds light on this problem.
mis.why: Say "shed light on" without "a" and with "on", not "about".

def: To protect someone or something from danger, harm, or harsh conditions.
ex: Wear tinted sunglasses to shield your eyes from bright ultraviolet sunlight during hikes.
nat: The manager shielded her junior developers from unreasonable executive deadline pressures.

mis.bad: This sunscreen shields your skin of sunburn.
mis.good: This sunscreen shields your skin from sunburn.
mis.why: Use "shield [someone/something] from [danger]", not "of".

def: To shine with a soft, slightly flickering or wavering light.
ex: Gentle ocean waves shimmered softly under the full moon along the tropical coastline.
nat: Her sequined silver dress shimmered brilliantly under the theater stage lights.

mis.bad: The water was shimmering with gold colors.
mis.good: The water was shimmering with golden light.
mis.why: Use "golden" as the descriptive adjective before light.

def: Having or showing sharp powers of judgment in practical or financial matters.
ex: Buying undervalued commercial property in that suburb was a remarkably shrewd business move.
nat: She is a shrewd negotiator who rarely concedes on contract price points.

mis.bad: He made a shrewdly decision yesterday.
mis.good: He made a shrewd decision yesterday.
mis.why: Use the adjective "shrewd" to modify a noun like "decision".

def: A place regarded as holy or sacred, dedicated to a deity or respected figure.
ex: Thousands of tourists quietly visit the historic Buddhist shrine in Kyoto each year.
nat: Fans created an impromptu candlelit shrine outside the rock star childhood home.

mis.bad: We visited to a shrine in Japan.
mis.good: We visited a shrine in Japan.
mis.why: "Visit" is a transitive verb in English; omit "to".

pt: estremecer / tremer de medo ou frio
def: To shake uncontrollably as a result of fear, cold, or strong disgust.
ex: I shudder to think how close we came to missing the final deadline.
nat: The old diesel locomotive shuddered violently before grinding to a complete halt.

mis.bad: I shudder thinking in that accident.
mis.good: I shudder to think of that accident.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "shudder to think of/about".

def: To mix playing cards or tracks randomly, or walk dragging one's feet.
ex: You should shuffle the cards thoroughly before dealing them to the players.
nat: Tired commuters shuffled slowly down the subway corridor during Monday morning rush.

mis.bad: Put the music on the shuffle.
mis.good: Put the music on shuffle.
mis.why: Say "on shuffle" without the article "the".

def: An activity done in addition to one's main job, or edge of a sports field.
ex: She started an online tutoring sideline that eventually replaced her full-time salary.
nat: The injured striker watched the entire championship final from the sideline.

mis.bad: He watched the game by the sidelines.
mis.good: He watched the game from the sidelines.
mis.why: Use "from the sidelines" to describe watching from the boundary.

def: A paved footpath along the side of a street for pedestrians.
ex: Outdoor dining tables occupied half of the wide concrete sidewalk along the avenue.
nat: Please do not ride electric rental scooters on the pedestrian sidewalk downtown.

mis.bad: Walk in the sidewalk to be safe.
mis.good: Walk on the sidewalk to be safe.
mis.why: Use the preposition "on the sidewalk", not "in".

def: To pass flour through a sieve, or examine information closely to find key facts.
ex: HR specialists had to sift through hundreds of resumes before picking final candidates.
nat: Always sift the flour before mixing it with melted butter and sugar.

mis.bad: We sifted the data to find anomalies.
mis.good: We sifted through the data to find anomalies.
mis.why: Use "sift through" when reviewing a large amount of information or data.

def: The dark shape and outline of someone or something visible against a lighter background.
ex: The iconic skyscraper cast a majestic silhouette against the colorful sunset horizon.
nat: I could only distinguish the dark silhouette of a person standing nearby.

mis.bad: I saw a silhouette on the window.
mis.good: I saw a silhouette in the window.
mis.why: Use "in the window" for someone or an outline framed by a window.

def: Occurring, operating, or done at the exact same time.
ex: The distributed server handled three thousand simultaneous database requests without dropping connections.
nat: The international conference provided simultaneous translation in four different official languages.

mis.bad: They occurred in a simultaneous time.
mis.good: They occurred at the same time / simultaneously.
mis.why: Use "at the same time" or the adverb "simultaneously".

def: Giving the impression that something harmful, evil, or threatening will happen.
ex: The sudden drop in internet speed had a more sinister cyberattack cause behind it.
nat: There was a sinister look in his eyes before he turned away.

mis.bad: The house was looking very sinister.
mis.good: The house looked very sinister.
mis.why: Stative sensory verbs like "look" normally take simple tense, not progressive.

def: An attitude of doubting the truth of something or claims made by others.
ex: Engineers greeted the ambitious product launch timeline with noticeable professional skepticism.
nat: Healthy scientific skepticism is essential when evaluating sensational health claims online.

mis.bad: He has skepticism of my idea.
mis.good: He has skepticism about my idea / is skeptical of my idea.
mis.why: Use "skepticism about" as a noun, or "skeptical of" as an adjective.

def: Not thorough or detailed, or giving suspicions of dishonesty or danger.
ex: Avoid entering personal credit card details on that sketchy e-commerce website.
nat: The preliminary design requirements are still sketchy and need further engineering refinement.

mis.bad: That offer seems too much sketchy.
mis.good: That offer seems too sketchy.
mis.why: Do not use "too much" before an adjective; use "too sketchy".

def: An outline of land and buildings defined against the sky.
ex: The observation deck offers an extraordinary panoramic view of the Manhattan skyline.
nat: Cranes and modern skyscrapers continue to transform the expanding city skyline.

mis.bad: I took photos of the skyline city.
mis.good: I took photos of the city skyline.
mis.why: Put the noun adjunct "city" before "skyline": "city skyline".

def: The action or crime of making a false spoken statement damaging someone.
ex: The politician sued the radio broadcaster for slander after defamatory remarks aired live.
nat: Spreading false allegations about coworkers can easily lead to serious slander charges.

mis.bad: He committed a slander against me.
mis.good: He committed slander / slandered me.
mis.why: "Slander" is usually uncountable; avoid "a slander".

pt: dar um tapa / estapear / impor bruscamente
def: To strike someone or something quickly with the palm of one's hand.
ex: The regulatory agency decided to slap heavy fines on the non-compliant corporation.
nat: He had to slap his alarm clock several times to turn it off.

mis.bad: The referee slapped to the player.
mis.good: The referee slapped the player.
mis.why: "Slap" is transitive; omit "to".

def: A fine-grained grey rock, a writing tablet, or a list of candidates.
ex: The progressive party announced a diverse slate of candidates for local council elections.
nat: Roofers carefully replaced the damaged slate tiles before the rainy season arrived.

mis.bad: Let us start from a white slate.
mis.good: Let us start with a clean slate.
mis.why: The common idiom is "clean slate", not "white slate".

def: The killing of animals for food, or brutal killing of many people.
ex: International human rights organizations condemned the senseless slaughter of innocent civilian refugees.
nat: Strict sanitary guidelines govern livestock slaughter in modern processing facilities.

mis.bad: The war caused a big slaughter.
mis.good: The war caused terrible slaughter / a massacre.
mis.why: "Slaughter" is often uncountable; use "terrible slaughter" or "a massacre".

def: Having no sleeves; having the arms completely bare.
ex: She prefers wearing lightweight sleeveless tops when running outside in the summer heat.
nat: A casual sleeveless dress is perfect for a warm beachside dinner.

mis.bad: I bought a shirt without sleeves.
mis.good: I bought a sleeveless shirt.
mis.why: "Sleeveless" is the standard natural compound adjective in English.

def: Gracefully thin, or barely sufficient in amount or degree.
ex: The candidate won the municipal mayoral election by a remarkably slender margin.
nat: The ballerina had a slender figure and moved across the stage effortlessly.

mis.bad: She has a very thin and slender body.
mis.good: She has a very slender figure.
mis.why: "Slender" already implies graceful thinness; avoid pairing with "thin".

def: To move smoothly along a surface while remaining in continuous contact.
ex: Be very careful when you slide down the snow-covered hill on your sled.
nat: Quarterly tech company profits continued to slide as enterprise software demand slowed.

mis.bad: I slided on the wet bathroom floor.
mis.good: I slid on the wet bathroom floor.
mis.why: Irregular verb: slide — slid — slid (not "slided").

def: Small in degree; not considerable or substantial.
ex: We experienced a slight delay in processing payments due to routine bank maintenance.
nat: There was a slight misunderstanding about who was leading the morning design review.

mis.bad: I do not have the smaller doubt.
mis.good: I do not have the slightest doubt.
mis.why: Use the idiom "not the slightest doubt", not "smaller doubt".

def: To a small degree or extent; a little bit.
ex: The latest software update is slightly faster than the previous stable release version.
nat: Her opinion on remote work shifted slightly after working abroad for six months.

mis.bad: The price is slightly more cheap.
mis.good: The price is slightly cheaper.
mis.why: Do not say "more cheap"; use the comparative form "cheaper".

def: Difficult to hold firmly or stand on because it is smooth or wet.
ex: The outdoor wooden deck becomes dangerously slippery whenever heavy rainfall covers the surface.
nat: Tax law loopholes can become a slippery slope leading toward illegal evasion.

mis.bad: The floor is very slipped.
mis.good: The floor is very slippery.
mis.why: Use the adjective "slippery", not the participle "slipped".

def: A short and striking or memorable phrase used in advertising or politics.
ex: The marketing agency crafted a catchy slogan to launch the new beverage line.
nat: Campaign volunteers printed the inspiring political slogan on hundreds of colorful banners.

mis.bad: They created a slogan very catchy.
mis.good: They created a very catchy slogan.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "a very catchy slogan".

def: A surface of which one end or side is at a higher level.
ex: Skiers raced enthusiastically down the steep snowy mountain slope during the winter festival.
nat: The gradual slope of the driveway makes wheelchair access easy for all residents.

mis.bad: Be careful on the slope steep.
mis.good: Be careful on the steep slope.
mis.why: Place the adjective "steep" before the noun "slope".

def: An overcrowded and squalid urban area inhabited by very poor people.
ex: Urban planners proposed affordable housing initiatives to rehabilitate the historic riverbank slum areas.
nat: Nonprofit organizations run education and health clinics inside several large municipal slums.

mis.bad: He lives in a slum neighborhood.
mis.good: He lives in a slum / informal settlement.
mis.why: "Slum" is already an urban area; avoid the redundant "slum neighborhood".

def: To break violently into pieces, or hit something forcefully.
ex: The unruly protestor attempted to smash the shop window with a heavy rock.
nat: The action blockbuster smashed previous box office opening weekend records across Latin America.

mis.bad: The car smashed in the wall.
mis.good: The car smashed into the wall.
mis.why: Use "smash into [an obstacle]", not "in".

pt: sorrir com ironia / dar sorriso amarelo
def: To smile in an irritatingly smug, conceited, or silly way.
ex: He could not help but smirk when his arrogant rival missed the target.
nat: She wiped the smirk off her face once the serious meeting officially began.

mis.bad: He smirked to me during the debate.
mis.good: He smirked at me during the debate.
mis.why: Use "smirk at [someone]", not "to".

def: Having or showing an excessive pride in oneself or one's achievements.
ex: Nobody liked his smug attitude after winning the company quarterly sales competition.
nat: She gave a smug smile after guessing the surprise ending of the mystery movie.

mis.bad: He looked very smugly after winning.
mis.good: He looked very smug after winning.
mis.why: Verbs of perception like "look" take predicate adjectives ("smug"), not adverbs.

def: To move goods or people illegally into or out of a country.
ex: Criminal gangs attempted to smuggle rare wildlife species across the international airport checkpoint.
nat: Border patrol officers caught a suspect trying to smuggle diamonds inside vintage watches.

mis.bad: They smuggled drugs for the country.
mis.good: They smuggled drugs into the country.
mis.why: Use "smuggle into [a place]", not "for".

pt: estalar / quebrar de repente / tirar foto
def: To break suddenly with a sharp crack, or take a quick casual photograph.
ex: Heavy winter ice caused the old oak branch to snap and crash onto the driveway.
nat: Tourists love to snap quick selfies in front of historic national landmarks.

mis.bad: He made a decision of snap.
mis.good: He made a snap decision.
mis.why: Use "snap decision" as a compound noun phrase.

def: To quickly seize something in a rude, eager, or aggressive manner.
ex: A cheeky monkey managed to snatch the tourist banana right out of her backpack.
nat: The home team snatched victory in the final seconds of extra time.

mis.bad: He snatched to my phone and ran.
mis.good: He snatched my phone and ran.
mis.why: "Snatch" takes a direct object without "to".

def: To move or go in a furtive, stealthy, or quiet manner.
ex: The mischievous puppy tried to sneak into the kitchen while we were having dinner.
nat: She managed to sneak a quick glance at her phone during the boring lecture.

mis.bad: He sneaked in the room without noise.
mis.good: He sneaked into the room quietly.
mis.why: Use "sneak into" to indicate movement inside.

pt: trecho / fragmento de código ou texto
def: A small piece or brief extract of information, code, or conversation.
ex: The developer pasted a helpful code snippet into the internal team Slack channel.
nat: I only overheard a brief snippet of their conversation in the hallway.

mis.bad: Can you send me that snip of code?
mis.good: Can you send me that code snippet?
mis.why: Use the standard noun "code snippet" for a small block of programming code.

def: Not intoxicated by alcohol, or serious, sensible, and solemn in tone.
ex: Always designate a sober driver before attending late evening celebrations with colleagues.
nat: The board delivered a sober assessment of company finances for the coming fiscal year.

mis.bad: He was completely sobriety yesterday.
mis.good: He was completely sober yesterday.
mis.why: Use the adjective "sober" after the linking verb "was", not the noun "sobriety".

def: To participate in social activities and mix socially with others.
ex: Remote engineers need intentional opportunities to socialize and build rapport with their teammates.
nat: She enjoys socializing with neighbors at the community garden on Saturday mornings.

mis.bad: I like to socialize with my friends in the weekend.
mis.good: I like to socialize with my friends on the weekend.
mis.why: In American English, use "on the weekend", not "in".

def: Comfort or consolation in a time of distress, grief, or sadness.
ex: Many people find solace in listening to classical music after an exhausting workday.
nat: She sought solace in long morning walks through the quiet botanical gardens.

mis.bad: Music gave a solace for me.
mis.good: Music gave me solace / brought me solace.
mis.why: "Solace" is typically uncountable; say "gave me solace".

def: Formal and dignified; serious and without humor or cheer.
ex: A solemn silence fell across the assembly as the memorial ceremony began.
nat: The newly elected president made a solemn promise to defend constitutional rights.

mis.bad: He gave an solemn speech.
mis.good: He gave a solemn speech.
mis.why: The "s" in "solemn" is a consonant sound, so use the article "a".

def: To ask for or try to obtain something from someone formally.
ex: The open-source maintainers actively solicit feedback from community developers on new features.
nat: Nonprofit organizations solicit charitable donations through annual direct mail fundraising campaigns.

mis.bad: The company solicited for customer reviews.
mis.good: The company solicited customer reviews.
mis.why: "Solicit" is transitive and takes a direct object without "for".

def: Done or existing alone; single or without companions.
ex: He enjoyed taking solitary evening walks along the deserted seashore to clear his mind.
nat: A solitary oak tree stood prominently in the center of the grassy pasture.

mis.bad: He prefers a life solitary.
mis.good: He prefers a solitary life.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "a solitary life".

def: The state or situation of being alone, especially when peaceful and pleasant.
ex: She valued the quiet solitude of her studio apartment after hectic days at work.
nat: Writers often retreat into peaceful solitude to concentrate on finishing their novels.

mis.bad: I feel very solitude when I travel alone.
mis.good: I feel very lonely when I travel alone / I enjoy solitude.
mis.why: "Solitude" is a noun meaning peaceful aloneness; for the sad feeling use the adjective "lonely".

def: Able to be dissolved, especially in water or another liquid solvent.
ex: Dietary fiber exists in two main forms, known as soluble and insoluble fiber.
nat: Sugar and table salt are both completely soluble in warm tap water.

mis.bad: This vitamin is soluble with water.
mis.good: This vitamin is soluble in water.
mis.why: Use the preposition "in" with "soluble", not "with".

def: To gently calm a person or feelings, or relieve bodily pain.
ex: Drinking warm chamomile tea can soothe a sore throat before you fall asleep.
nat: Soft classical lullabies helped soothe the crying infant during the turbulent flight.

mis.bad: This cream soothes of skin burns.
mis.good: This cream soothes skin burns.
mis.why: "Soothe" takes a direct object without "of".

def: A feeling of deep distress caused by loss, disappointment, or major misfortune.
ex: The entire community expressed profound sorrow over the unexpected passing of the doctor.
nat: Time gradually helped heal the sorrow she felt after losing her childhood home.

mis.bad: He felt a big sorrow for the news.
mis.good: He felt deep sorrow at the news.
mis.why: Use "deep sorrow at/over", not "a big sorrow for".

def: Possessing supreme or ultimate power, or acting as an independent state.
ex: Every sovereign nation has the legal authority to control its own international borders.
nat: The government established a sovereign wealth fund to manage surplus oil revenues.

mis.bad: Brazil is an sovereign republic.
mis.good: Brazil is a sovereign republic.
mis.why: Pronounce "sovereign" as /ˈsɑːvrɪn/ with a consonant sound, so use "a".

def: Supreme power or authority; the authority of a state to govern itself.
ex: The treaty guarantees the territorial integrity and national sovereignty of all member states.
nat: Data sovereignty regulations require user records to remain stored within national borders.

mis.bad: The country defends their sovereignty.
mis.good: The country defends its sovereignty.
mis.why: A country is referred to with the singular neuter possessive "its", not "their".

def: To extend across a period of time or physical distance.
ex: Her impressive academic research career spanned more than four decades across three universities.
nat: The suspension bridge spans the entire width of the wide coastal bay.

mis.bad: The conference spanned through three days.
mis.good: The conference spanned three days.
mis.why: "Span" is transitive and does not take the preposition "through".

def: To ignite a fire, or trigger a sudden event, debate, or emotion.
ex: The controversial policy announcement sparked intense debate across the company internal message boards.
nat: A stray electrical spark ignited dry brush along the edge of the forest.

mis.bad: His speech sparked up many questions.
mis.good: His speech sparked many questions.
mis.why: Do not add "up" to "spark" when meaning trigger or cause.

def: To shine brightly with flashes of light, or be lively and witty.
ex: The freshly fallen snow sparkled brilliantly under the clear morning winter sunshine.
nat: Her eyes sparkled with excitement when she heard the wonderful family news.

mis.bad: I prefer water with gas than sparkling water.
mis.good: I prefer sparkling water to still water.
mis.why: In English, use "sparkling water" rather than literal "water with gas".

def: Thinly dispersed or scattered; existing only in small amounts.
ex: Vegetation is extremely sparse across the arid rocky plains of the desert.
nat: Official attendance at the morning keynote lecture was disappointingly sparse today.

mis.bad: The data in the table are very sparse.
mis.good: The data in the table is very sparse.
mis.why: In modern computing English, "data" is commonly treated as a singular mass noun.

def: To produce eggs, or generate a rapid series of similar things.
ex: The breakthrough smartphone design spawned countless copycat products across global electronics markets.
nat: Every spring, salmon swim upstream to spawn in cool freshwater mountain rivers.

mis.bad: The script spawns up a new child process.
mis.good: The script spawns a new child process.
mis.why: Omit "up"; the technical verb is simply "spawn a process".

def: To form a theory or conjecture without firm evidence, or invest with risk.
ex: Financial analysts continue to speculate about whether interest rates will decline next quarter.
nat: It is useless to speculate on the root cause before reviewing system logs.

mis.bad: We should not speculate of what happened.
mis.good: We should not speculate on what happened.
mis.why: Use "speculate on" or "speculate about", not "of".

def: The forming of a theory or conjecture without firm evidence.
ex: Rampant market speculation drove the stock price far beyond its fundamental asset valuation.
nat: Her sudden resignation fueled intense media speculation about internal leadership conflicts.

mis.bad: These are only speculations without proof.
mis.good: This is merely speculation without proof.
mis.why: "Speculation" is usually used as an uncountable mass noun.

def: Shaped like a sphere; completely round in three dimensions.
ex: Most planets and large celestial bodies assume an approximately spherical shape over time.
nat: The futuristic museum building features a massive spherical auditorium in the center.

mis.bad: The Earth has a form spherical.
mis.good: The Earth has a spherical shape.
mis.why: Put the adjective before the noun: "a spherical shape".

def: To move in a continuous curve, or increase/decrease rapidly out of control.
ex: Project costs can quickly spiral out of control without strict daily budget oversight.
nat: Smoke continued to spiral upward from the extinguished campsite fire pit.

mis.bad: The inflation spiraled to up last year.
mis.good: Inflation spiraled upward last year.
mis.why: Use "spiraled upward" or "spiraled out of control", not "spiraled to up".

def: To cause liquid to scatter in flying drops, or fall into water.
ex: Be careful not to splash cold water on the electrical outlets while cleaning.
nat: Playful children splashed merrily in the lake during the warm summer afternoon.

mis.bad: He splashed water to my shirt.
mis.good: He splashed water on my shirt.
mis.why: Use "splash [liquid] on [a surface]", not "to".

def: Magnificent; very impressive, excellent, or grand in scale.
ex: The hotel rooftop terrace offers a splendid view of the illuminated city monuments.
nat: We spent a splendid afternoon exploring the botanical gardens with visiting relatives.

mis.bad: We had a splendid time together yesterday.
mis.good: We had a splendid time together yesterday.
mis.why: Remember "splendid" expresses warm British and formal American enthusiasm.

def: A small, thin, sharp piece of wood, glass, or metal broken off.
ex: Be careful walking barefoot on the weathered wooden boardwalk or you might get a splinter.
nat: A tiny glass splinter lodged in the palm of his hand while cleaning.

mis.bad: I took out an splinter from my finger.
mis.good: I pulled a splinter out of my finger.
mis.why: Use the article "a" before consonant sound /s/: "a splinter".

def: Performed or occurring as a result of a sudden impulse without premeditation.
ex: The comedian warm jokes prompted spontaneous laughter and enthusiastic applause from the audience.
nat: We took a spontaneous weekend road trip to the coast without booking hotels.

mis.bad: It was an decision very spontaneous.
mis.good: It was a very spontaneous decision.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "a very spontaneous decision".

def: A lamp projecting a narrow intense beam of light, or center of attention.
ex: The young startup found itself in the international media spotlight after securing funding.
nat: Stage technicians turned the main spotlight directly toward the lead singer center stage.

mis.bad: He does not like being on the spotlight.
mis.good: He does not like being in the spotlight.
mis.why: The natural idiom is "in the spotlight", not "on".

def: An ungainly or carelessly spread-out mass, especially rapid suburban development.
ex: Urban planners aim to contain urban sprawl by improving inner-city high-density public transport.
nat: The sprawling city covers hundreds of square kilometers across the valley basin.

mis.bad: The city has an excessive sprawl urban.
mis.good: The city has excessive urban sprawl.
mis.why: Put the adjective "urban" before the noun "sprawl": "urban sprawl".

def: To scatter small drops of liquid or particles of a substance over something.
ex: Lightly sprinkle fresh grated parmesan cheese over the pasta before serving the dinner.
nat: A light rain began to sprinkle just as we finished packing the car.

mis.bad: Sprinkle with sugar the cake.
mis.good: Sprinkle the cake with sugar / sprinkle sugar on the cake.
mis.why: Use "sprinkle [substance] on [something]" or "sprinkle [something] with [substance]".

def: To produce shoots or new growth, or start growing or developing rapidly.
ex: Bean seeds usually sprout within four or five days when placed in damp soil.
nat: New specialty coffee shops have started to sprout all over our neighborhood recently.

mis.bad: The seeds are sprouting up on the ground.
mis.good: The seeds are sprouting up from the ground.
mis.why: Use "sprout from the ground", not "on".

def: To urge on or encourage an action, development, or economic growth.
ex: Lower interest rates helped spur business investment and new consumer housing construction.
nat: Curiosity and personal ambition spurred her to learn full-stack software development independently.

mis.bad: They decided on the spur of moment.
mis.good: They decided on the spur of the moment.
mis.why: Include the definite article: "on the spur of the moment".

def: Not being what it purports to be; false, illegitimate, or fake.
ex: The defense attorney dismissed the allegations as completely spurious claims designed to distract.
nat: The sensor generated spurious readings due to electromagnetic interference along the wiring.

mis.bad: He presented a spurious proof.
mis.good: He presented spurious evidence / a false claim.
mis.why: "Proof" is uncountable in English; use "spurious evidence".

def: To waste money, time, or an opportunity in a reckless or foolish manner.
ex: The team cannot afford to squander this unique opportunity to capture international market share.
nat: He managed to squander his inheritance within two years on luxury sports cars.

mis.bad: Do not squander with your money.
mis.good: Do not squander your money.
mis.why: "Squander" is transitive and takes a direct object without "with".

def: To crush or squeeze something flat, or suppress a rebellion or rumor.
ex: Be careful packing your luggage so you do not accidentally squash your sunglasses.
nat: The company spokesperson moved quickly to squash rumors of an impending hostile takeover.

mis.bad: The car squashed on my box.
mis.good: The car squashed my box.
mis.why: "Squash" does not take the preposition "on"; it takes a direct object.

def: To make a high-pitched sound or cry, or succeed by a narrow margin.
ex: The front wooden door began to squeak loudly every time someone opened it.
nat: The home basketball team managed to squeak through to the semifinals with one point.

mis.bad: The door makes an squeak noise.
mis.good: The door makes a squeaky noise / a squeak.
mis.why: Use "a squeak" or the adjective "a squeaky noise".

def: To firmly press something from opposite sides, or extract juice by pressing.
ex: You should squeeze fresh lime juice over the grilled fish right before eating.
nat: Rising office rental prices continue to squeeze profit margins for small retail businesses.

mis.bad: I squeezed out of the orange.
mis.good: I squeezed the orange.
mis.why: Use "squeeze [fruit]" to extract juice, or "squeeze juice out of [fruit]".

pt: apertar os olhos / olhar de soslaio
def: To look at someone or something with eyes partly closed.
ex: Bright glare from the afternoon sun forced the driver to squint through the windshield.
nat: He had to squint at the tiny font on the printed contract paper.

mis.bad: I had to squint my eyes to read.
mis.good: I had to squint to read.
mis.why: "Squint" already implies narrowing the eyes; "squint my eyes" is slightly redundant.

def: To thrust a knife or other pointed weapon into someone or something.
ex: The chef used a sharp stainless steel fork to stab the roasting potatoes.
nat: He decided to take a stab at writing his first technical tutorial online.

mis.bad: He gave a stab on the problem.
mis.good: He took a stab at the problem.
mis.why: The common idiom for attempting something is "take a stab at".

def: To walk unsteadily, or arrange events at different times, or astonish someone.
ex: The company decided to stagger employee arrival times to ease peak hour elevator congestion.
nat: He was so exhausted from the marathon that he began to stagger forward.

mis.bad: We staggered the meetings in five minutes.
mis.good: We staggered the meetings by five minutes.
mis.why: Use "by" to express the time interval when staggering events.

def: To pursue or approach quarry stealthily, or harass someone with unwanted surveillance.
ex: Lions quietly stalk their prey through tall savannah grass before launching an attack.
nat: Cybersecurity specialists warn users never to stalk or harass individuals across social media.

mis.bad: He stalked to his ex-girlfriend online.
mis.good: He stalked his ex-girlfriend online.
mis.why: "Stalk" takes a direct object without "to".

def: To stop running unexpectedly (engine), or delay an action or process deliberately.
ex: Contract negotiations began to stall over intellectual property rights and developer equity shares.
nat: The manual car engine will stall if you release the clutch pedal too abruptly.

mis.bad: The car stalled down on the hill.
mis.good: The car stalled on the hill.
mis.why: Do not say "stalled down"; simply say "stalled".

def: A small piece of paper stuck to mail, or an ink impression tool.
ex: Do not forget to affix a valid postal stamp before dropping the envelope.
nat: Customs immigration officers stamped his travel passport with a three-month tourist visa.

mis.bad: I bought a postal stamp for five dollars.
mis.good: I bought a postage stamp for five dollars.
mis.why: The standard collocation in English is "postage stamp", not "postal stamp".

def: Able to operate independently of other systems or components without external support.
ex: The company launched a standalone mobile app that does not require desktop login.
nat: Security engineers deployed a standalone firewall appliance to protect sensitive database backups.

mis.bad: It is an app stand-alone.
mis.good: It is a standalone app.
mis.why: Adjectives precede nouns in English: "a standalone app".

def: A group of lines forming the basic recurring metrical unit in poetry.
ex: The English teacher asked students to analyze the rhythmic structure of each stanza.
nat: The second stanza of the famous romantic poem expresses deep longing and grief.

mis.bad: The poetry has five strophes.
mis.good: The poem has five stanzas.
mis.why: In English poetry analysis, use "stanza", not Portuguese-influenced "strophe".

def: A wire fastener, or a main or essential element of something.
ex: Rice and black beans remain the quintessential dietary staple across all Brazilian households.
nat: Daily standup meetings have become a staple of modern agile software development teams.

mis.bad: Beans are an staple in Brazil.
mis.good: Beans are a staple in Brazil.
mis.why: The initial "s" is a consonant sound, so use the article "a".

def: The state or status of being a famous performer or celebrity.
ex: The talented young singer rose to international stardom after her viral video performance.
nat: Sudden stardom can create immense psychological pressure for young professional athletes and actors.

mis.bad: She arrived to the stardom very fast.
mis.good: She rose to stardom very quickly.
mis.why: Use the collocation "rose to stardom", not "arrived to".

def: Severe or bare in appearance; sharply clear and impossible to avoid.
ex: The latest audit report revealed a stark contrast between corporate promises and reality.
nat: The desert landscape presented a stark beauty under the blazing afternoon sun.

mis.bad: There is an stark difference between them.
mis.good: There is a stark difference between them.
mis.why: Use the article "a" before the consonant sound /st/: "a stark difference".

def: To cause a person or animal to feel sudden shock or alarm.
ex: The sudden loud ring of the fire alarm managed to startle everyone inside.
nat: Try not to make abrupt movements that might startle the nervous rescue dog.

mis.bad: The thunder startled to me.
mis.good: The thunder startled me.
mis.why: "Startle" is transitive and takes a direct object without "to".

def: Lacking in movement, action, or change, especially in an uninteresting way.
ex: Modern web developers rarely build completely static websites without dynamic content rendering pipelines.
nat: Oil prices remained static throughout the summer due to steady international supply agreements.

mis.bad: The code analyzer does an static checking.
mis.good: The code analyzer does a static check / static analysis.
mis.why: Use the article "a" before /st/: "a static analysis".

def: Not moving, or not intended to be moved; staying in place.
ex: Riding a stationary bicycle at the gym provides an excellent cardiovascular indoor workout.
nat: The vehicle remained stationary at the red traffic light until pedestrians crossed safely.

mis.bad: The car was stationated near the corner.
mis.good: The car was stationary / parked near the corner.
mis.why: Do not confuse the adjective "stationary" with Portuguese "estacionado" (parked).

def: Writing materials, including paper, envelopes, pens, and related office supplies.
ex: The administrative assistant ordered fresh corporate stationery printed with the updated company logo.
nat: You can purchase pens, folders, and notebooks in the college stationery store downstairs.

mis.bad: I bought some stationaries yesterday.
mis.good: I bought some stationery yesterday.
mis.why: "Stationery" (with an e) is uncountable and never takes a plural form.

def: A written law passed by a legislative body or governing authority.
ex: The criminal charge was dismissed because the applicable statute of limitations had expired.
nat: Federal statute requires financial institutions to report suspicious customer cash transactions promptly.

mis.bad: The crime was prohibited by statute limitations.
mis.good: The crime was prohibited by the statute of limitations.
mis.why: Say "the statute of limitations" with both definite articles and "of".

def: Required, permitted, or enacted by written statute or official law.
ex: Employees in the tech sector are entitled to thirty days of statutory paid leave.
nat: The board of directors met all statutory audit requirements before the annual deadline.

mis.bad: It is an statutory rule in this state.
mis.good: It is a statutory rule in this state.
mis.why: Use the article "a" before the consonant sound /st/: "a statutory rule".

def: Loyal and committed in attitude; firm and steadfast in support.
ex: The senior engineer remained a staunch advocate of thorough automated testing and documentation.
nat: She has been a staunch supporter of open-source software libraries for decades.

mis.bad: He is a staunchly defender of privacy.
mis.good: He is a staunch defender of privacy.
mis.why: Use the adjective "staunch" before the noun "defender".

def: Resolutely or dutifully firm and unwavering in loyalty or determination.
ex: Despite harsh public criticism, the startup founder remained steadfast in his long-term product vision.
nat: Her steadfast commitment to social justice inspired colleagues across the entire non-profit organization.

mis.bad: He stayed steadfastly during the trial.
mis.good: He remained steadfast during the trial.
mis.why: Use the adjective "steadfast" after linking verbs like "remained" or "stayed".

def: Cautious and surreptitious action or movement designed to avoid detection.
ex: Military radar systems struggle to detect modern stealth aircraft flying at low altitudes.
nat: The technology startup operated in stealth mode for eighteen months before public launch.

mis.bad: The startup works in mode stealth.
mis.good: The startup works in stealth mode.
mis.why: Adjective/noun adjuncts precede the head noun in English: "stealth mode".

def: Serious and unrelenting, especially in the assertion of authority and discipline.
ex: The project manager issued a stern warning regarding missed sprint deadlines and communication.
nat: He had a stern facial expression that made junior team members feel intimidated.

mis.bad: She gave to him a stern look.
mis.good: She gave him a stern look.
mis.why: Use "gave him a stern look" without the preposition "to".

def: To make someone unable to breathe properly, or restrain or suppress an idea.
ex: Excessive micromanagement and red tape will quickly stifle creative innovation in engineering teams.
nat: She tried to stifle a yawn during the lengthy quarterly earnings slide presentation.

mis.bad: The hot air stifled to me.
mis.good: The hot air stifled me.
mis.why: "Stifle" is transitive and takes a direct object without "to".

def: To raise levels of physiological or nervous activity in the body or mind.
ex: Engaging technical puzzles can effectively stimulate brain activity and enhance creative problem-solving skills.
nat: The central government cut tax rates to stimulate domestic manufacturing and consumer spending.

mis.bad: Coffee stimulates to my brain in morning.
mis.good: Coffee stimulates my brain in the morning.
mis.why: "Stimulate" is transitive; do not insert "to" before the direct object.

def: A thing or event that evokes a specific functional reaction in an organ.
ex: Government economic stimulus packages helped small businesses survive during the prolonged mandatory lockdown.
nat: Visual stimulus can trigger rapid memory recall during foreign language vocabulary study sessions.

mis.bad: The government approved three stimulus.
mis.good: The government approved three stimulus packages / stimuli.
mis.why: The plural of "stimulus" is "stimuli" (/ˈstɪmjəlaɪ/) or use "stimulus packages".

def: To demand or specify a requirement, typically as part of a formal agreement.
ex: The service agreement stipulates that system maintenance must occur during weekend overnight hours.
nat: Federal laws stipulate minimum safety precautions for all industrial construction job sites.

mis.bad: The contract stipulates about the delivery date.
mis.good: The contract stipulates the delivery date / stipulates that...
mis.why: "Stipulate" is transitive and does not take "about".

def: A condition or requirement that is specified or demanded as part of an agreement.
ex: The investor agreement included a strict stipulation that the founders retain majority equity control.
nat: One key stipulation in the commercial lease prohibited subletting without prior landlord approval.

mis.bad: He agreed with one stipulation: to finish early.
mis.good: He agreed with one stipulation: that we finish early.
mis.why: Use "with the stipulation that [clause]" to specify the condition.

def: A loop of thread or yarn resulting from a single pass or suture.
ex: The emergency room doctor placed three small stitches to close the minor forehead laceration.
nat: She picked up her knitting needle to correct a dropped stitch in the woolen scarf.

mis.bad: The doctor took five points in my arm.
mis.good: The doctor gave me five stitches in my arm.
mis.why: In medical English, use "stitches", not literal translation "points".

def: To accumulate a large stock of goods or materials for emergency use.
ex: Hospitals began to stockpile essential medical protective supplies ahead of the projected winter flu surge.
nat: During economic uncertainty, many households choose to stockpile nonperishable canned groceries at home.

mis.bad: They stockpiled of food for winter.
mis.good: They stockpiled food for winter.
mis.why: "Stockpile" is transitive; do not use "of" after the verb.

def: Uncomplicated and easy to do or understand; honest and frank in manner.
ex: The software installation process was completely straightforward and took less than two minutes.
nat: Her feedback was straightforward, practical, and helped the team improve immediately.

mis.bad: The solution is very straight forward.
mis.good: The solution is very straightforward.
mis.why: Write "straightforward" as a single unified word, not two separate words.

def: Showing signs of nervous tension, or not relaxed and natural.
ex: Relations between the two cofounders became increasingly strained following the product launch delay.
nat: She gave a strained smile and tried to change the awkward subject during lunch.

mis.bad: The relationship is strained with they.
mis.good: The relationship between them is strained.
mis.why: Say "the relationship between them is strained".

def: A narrow passage of water connecting two seas or large water areas.
ex: Commercial container ships pass daily through the narrow strait connecting the two oceans.
nat: The unexpected bankruptcy of their main client left the company in dire financial straits.

mis.bad: The family is in dire straight.
mis.good: The family is in dire straits.
mis.why: Do not confuse the noun "straits" (difficulties/water passage) with "straight" (direct/not curved).
